title: Reading the Morning Fog
subject: rla
passage:
Fog can make a familiar road feel newly uncertain. Buildings fade, traffic lights seem to float without poles, and distances become difficult to judge. Yet fog is not simply a cloud that has fallen by accident. It forms when air near the ground becomes cool enough for water vapor to condense into tiny droplets.

Different conditions can produce that cooling. On clear nights, the ground may lose heat rapidly and cool the air above it. In coastal areas, moist air can move over colder land or water. Valleys can also collect cooler, denser air. Because the process depends on local temperature, moisture, wind, and terrain, fog can be stubbornly local: one neighborhood may have clear skies while another, only a few kilometers away, is wrapped in gray.

That local behavior makes forecasting difficult. Weather models can predict the broad ingredients for fog, but the exact timing and thickness may depend on small changes that are hard to measure. A light breeze can mix the air enough to prevent fog in one place while leaving it untouched elsewhere.

For drivers, the most important feature of fog is not its scientific elegance but its effect on visibility. Bright headlights can actually make dense fog harder to see through because light reflects from the suspended droplets. Lower beams and reduced speed are often more useful than simply adding brightness.

Fog therefore rewards a particular kind of caution. It hides distance without stopping movement. The road is still there; the problem is that the driver can no longer read it as easily.
